$comment: SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for the KBS1 binary-value ENVELOPE — the wire that carries first-class byte-stream fields across the guest<->host capability seam (platform requirement R2: a contract-level 'this field is a byte stream' so host:store/host:net can take and return a Uint8Array/ptr+len instead of a JSON number-array). Full rationale, the current-flow audit, the QuickJS $b64 sidecar, the SDK wrappers and the phased plan live in store-net-bytes.DESIGN.md; THIS file locks only the on-the-wire ENVELOPE (magic, framing, sentinel, caps). It is a THIRD sibling to op-batch-wire.json (UI-tree diffs, magic 'KEEL') and canvas-wire.json (per-frame draw list, magic 'KCNV'); it shares their 'schema single-source + golden-lock + generated Rust constants' discipline (build.rs generate_store_net_contract + store-net-bytes.golden.json + store-net-bytes.CONFORMANCE.md) but is DELIBERATELY a different SHAPE: op-batch/canvas are opcode streams with a 16-byte header + intern table; KBS1 is a generic two-plane frame — a JSON CONTROL PLANE plus a length-prefixed BINARY DATA PLANE (multipart-like) — and is contract-agnostic (the codec walks the JSON for sentinels; it needs no per-call descriptor). CRITICAL magic discipline: 'KBS1' (4B 42 53 31) differs from 'KEEL' (4B 45 45 4C) at byte 1 and from 'KCNV' (4B 43 4E 56) at byte 1 too, so the host's first-byte/magic fork (all three start 0x4B 'K') routes a frame to exactly one decoder by comparing the FULL u32 — a frame meant for one fails the others' magic compare fail-closed before any field is read. Every codec MUST generate its constants FROM or validate them AGAINST this file, never hand-copy from a peer. All integers are UNSIGNED and LITTLE-ENDIAN.

magic.$comment: First 4 bytes of every KBS1 frame, read as a u32 LE. The bytes 4B 42 53 31 are ASCII 'K' 'B' 'S' '1' = 'Keel Binary Segments, version 1'. The u32 value 0x3153424b read little-endian yields exactly those bytes in order. DISTINCT from op-batch 0x4c45454b ('KEEL') and canvas 0x564e434b ('KCNV'): all three share byte 0 (0x4B 'K') but differ at byte 1 (0x42 'B' vs 0x45 'E' vs 0x43 'C'), so a u32 magic compare — which the host fork MUST use, never just byte 0 — disambiguates all three immediately. A decoder MUST read a u32 LE and reject fail-closed (reason 'bad-magic') if it is not exactly this value. THE VERSION RIDES THE 4TH MAGIC BYTE ('1' = 0x31): a v2 wire is 'KBS2' (0x3253424b), a different u32, so a v1 decoder rejects it on the SAME magic compare — there is NO separate version field on the wire (mirrors the canvas 'distinct magic' discipline; unlike op-batch/canvas which additionally carry a u16 protocolVersion, KBS1 folds version into the magic to keep the two-plane frame minimal).
magic.versionByte: the 4th ASCII byte ('1' = 0x31) IS the wire version; bump it (to '2' = 'KBS2') on any breaking framing change so an old decoder rejects a new frame on the magic compare.

protocolVersion.$comment: Documentation/codegen mirror of the version that rides the 4th magic byte ('1'). There is NO separate protocolVersion field ON THE WIRE (see magic.versionByte) — this block exists so build.rs can emit a PROTOCOL_VERSION constant alongside MAGIC (parity with the op-batch/canvas generators) and so a reader has one named place for 'which RBS version is this'. A v2 wire changes BOTH the 4th magic byte AND this value together.

framing.$comment: The complete on-the-wire byte layout. SYMMETRIC: the exact same framing is used in BOTH directions — guest->host request args AND host->guest return value. There is no header struct and no intern table (unlike op-batch/canvas): a frame is just magic, then a length-prefixed JSON control plane, then a length-prefixed list of raw binary segments. All lengths are u32 LE. Total framing overhead is 12 bytes + 4 bytes per segment (magic 4 + jsonLen 4 + segCount 4 + segLen 4*segCount).

byteLayout.name: magic
byteLayout.note: 0x3153424b = bytes 4B 42 53 31 = 'KBS1'. Reject on mismatch (reason 'bad-magic'). The 4th byte carries the version; there is no separate version field.

byteLayout.name: jsonLen
byteLayout.note: UTF-8 byte length of the JSON control plane that follows. MUST be validated against the remaining buffer BEFORE the JSON is read (reason 'truncated') and against limits.maxJsonBytes (reason 'json-too-big') — never trusted, never wrapped.

byteLayout.name: json
byteLayout.note: the UTF-8 JSON control plane. Holds every non-binary field verbatim; each byte-stream field is REPLACED by the {"$b":N} sentinel (see sentinel). No terminator; length is exactly jsonLen. MUST parse as JSON after length validation, else fail-closed (reason 'bad-json').

byteLayout.name: segCount
byteLayout.note: number of binary segments that follow. MUST be validated against limits.maxSegments (reason 'too-many-segments') BEFORE any segment is read. Every {"$b":N} sentinel in the JSON MUST reference an N in [0, segCount) (reason 'bad-segment-ref').

byteLayout.name: segments
byteLayout.note: segCount segments, tightly packed, in EMISSION ORDER (segment index = position, 0-based). Each is a (segLen u32, segLen raw bytes) pair. Segment index N is what a {"$b":N} sentinel resolves to.

record.name: segLen
record.note: byte length of this segment's raw payload. Validated against the remaining buffer (reason 'truncated') and limits.maxSegmentBytes (reason 'segment-too-big') BEFORE the bytes are read.

record.name: bytes
record.note: the raw byte stream, verbatim, no encoding and no terminator. Arbitrary bytes including 0x00 and 0xFF ride untouched — the control-plane JSON never holds the bytes, only the sentinel. On decode this becomes the field's Uint8Array; on encode a Uint8Array is hoisted here.

framing.strictTrailing: A decoder reads exactly segCount segments after the JSON and MUST then have fully consumed the buffer — ZERO bytes may remain (reason 'truncated' on either underrun OR trailing bytes). A frame is exactly its magic + control plane + declared segments; the encoder writes nothing after the final segment.
framing.atomicity: FAIL-CLOSED / whole-frame: on ANY violation the codec aborts the ENTIRE frame and lets nothing partial cross the seam. A decoder revives all sentinels into an in-memory value and hands it on only if the whole frame is valid — never a half-decoded value; an encoder throws before/without emitting a truncated buffer.

sentinel.$comment: How a byte-stream field appears in the JSON control plane and how the codec moves bytes between the two planes. The wire is SELF-DESCRIBING: the codec needs no per-call descriptor — it walks the parsed JSON for sentinels on decode and walks the value for Uint8Array on encode.
sentinel.rule: A byte-stream field's value in the JSON control plane is an object whose reserved key '$b' maps to EITHER (a) a single 0-based unsigned integer N — the index of the one segment carrying that field's bytes — OR (b) a NON-EMPTY ARRAY of such integers [N0, N1, …], meaning the field's bytes are the CONCATENATION of those segments in exactly that order. DECODE: the codec walks the parsed JSON and replaces every sentinel with its field's bytes (a Uint8Array / owned byte slice) — segment N for form (a), the ordered join for form (b). ENCODE: the codec walks the value, hoists every byte-stream value to NEW segments (appended in walk order) and replaces it with the sentinel naming those indices. Every index MUST be in [0, segCount) (reason 'bad-segment-ref'); each segment MUST be referenced at most once ACROSS THE WHOLE FRAME, including within a single array (reason 'bad-segment-ref'); an empty array, a non-integer element, or any other shape under the '$b' key is a malformed sentinel (reason 'bad-sentinel').
sentinel.reservedKey: '$b' is a RESERVED key: inside a KBS1 frame's control plane, an object of the exact shape {"$b": <non-negative integer>} — or {"$b": [<non-negative integer>, …]} — is ALWAYS interpreted as a segment reference, never as literal application data. See backCompat for why this reservation cannot collide with existing JSON-only calls.
sentinel.quickjsNote: The WASM boundary uses this index sentinel ({"$b":N}) with real length-prefixed segments. The QuickJS shell is a JSON-string bridge that cannot carry raw segment bytes, so on THAT transport a sibling inline sentinel {"$b64":"<base64>"} is used instead (see store-net-bytes.DESIGN.md §B.5). Both deliver a Uint8Array to the SAME handler; '$b64' is likewise a reserved key on the QuickJS path. KBS1 (this file) locks ONLY the WASM index form.
sentinel.multiSegmentValues: Form (b) is what lets ONE LOGICAL VALUE exceed limits.maxSegmentBytes. That cap bounds a single SEGMENT — one decoder allocation — and before form (b) existed it was therefore ALSO the ceiling on one stored value, which ordinary documents reach: a 1076x722 two-layer raster serialises to 3,956,173 bytes, and the largest two-layer document that fit under 1 MiB was 236x158. Splitting a value across segments keeps every INDIVIDUAL allocation bounded by maxSegmentBytes while lifting the ceiling on the value — and, the part a consumer cannot do for itself, keeps the value ATOMIC: it is one field of one frame, so the existing whole-frame fail-closed rule already covers it. Chunking in the application instead turns one value into meta + chunk/<n> keys whose compare-and-swap is PER KEY, so there is no way to version the SET, and a partial write leaves a torn value that only the application can detect.
sentinel.multiSegmentCeiling: NO new cap is introduced for a multi-segment value, deliberately: the concatenated allocation is already bounded by limits.maxEnvelopeBytes, which is validated against the WHOLE buffer before any decoding, and one value's segments cannot outweigh the frame carrying them. So the ceiling on one logical value is 'what the envelope cap allows' (4 MiB minus the control plane and the 12 + 4*segCount framing bytes), and maxEnvelopeBytes — NOT maxSegmentBytes — is now the binding constraint. A cap restating that arithmetic would never fire, so adding one would be dead weight. Note the peak decoder residency this implies: the frame plus the joined value, i.e. up to 2x maxEnvelopeBytes, because the segment bytes are COPIED into the joined value rather than aliased.
sentinel.multiSegmentEncoderRule: An encoder MUST emit form (a) for any value that fits in ONE segment, and MUST NOT emit a single-element array. A hard conformance requirement, not a style preference: it makes every frame expressible before this extension byte-for-byte IDENTICAL to before — so the pre-existing golden vectors still lock — and it means a value a peer could already carry is never re-encoded into a shape that peer may not understand. A decoder MUST still ACCEPT a single-element array, since rejecting it would be stricter than the grammar.
sentinel.oldDecoderBehaviour: This is an ADDITIVE grammar extension, so the magic stays 'KBS1': the FRAMING (magic, jsonLen, json, segCount, segments) is unchanged, and magic.versionByte is bumped only for a breaking FRAMING change. A decoder predating form (b) that meets a form-(b) frame rejects it FAIL-CLOSED with reason 'bad-sentinel' — it requires '$b' to map to a non-negative integer, and an array is not one — so it can never MISREAD such a frame as data. Combined with multiSegmentEncoderRule this means no call that worked before can regress: form (b) is only ever emitted for a value that exceeded maxSegmentBytes, which an old peer refused outright anyway.

backCompat.$comment: The load-bearing conformance invariant that lets KBS1 coexist with today's raw-JSON capability wire without touching a single existing call.
backCompat.invariant: A call OR return that carries NO binary segments MUST NOT use the KBS1 envelope. It stays byte-for-byte IDENTICAL to today's raw-JSON path: a plain UTF-8 JSON body beginning with '{' (0x7B) or '[' (0x5B). Only a call whose contract declares a binary field, AND only when that specific call/return actually carries at least one byte-stream value, is wrapped in a KBS1 frame.
backCompat.hostFork: The host's guest->host fork keys on the payload's leading bytes: 0x4B 'K' + full-u32 magic 'KBS1' -> the envelope codec; 0x4B 'K' + 'KCNV' -> canvas; 0x4B 'K' + 'KEEL' -> op-batch; anything else (a plain JSON body starts with '{' 0x7B or '[' 0x5B, which matches no magic) -> the existing JSON.parse path, unchanged. The fork MUST compare the full u32 magic, never a single byte, because all three binary magics share byte 0.
backCompat.returnFork: Symmetric on the return: a host result with no byte-stream value is JSON.stringify'd exactly as today (byte-for-byte identical reply); only a result carrying a Uint8Array is emitted as a KBS1 frame. A guest decoding a return treats a body whose first u32 is not the KBS1 magic as a plain-JSON reply.
backCompat.collisionClaim: Because pure-JSON calls are NEVER sentinel-walked (they never enter the envelope codec), a literal {"$b":N} in an existing call's data is inert — it can only be MISread as a sentinel INSIDE a KBS1 frame, i.e. only within a binary-declared call, where '$b' is a reserved key by contract. So the reservation introduces zero risk to any existing capability.
backCompat.conformanceRequirement: A conformant implementation MUST NOT emit a KBS1 frame for a segment-free call/return, and a golden/back-compat test MUST assert that an existing text capability's on-wire bytes are unchanged from a pre-change golden (the KBS1 fork is never taken for a non-binary call).

limits.$comment: FAIL-CLOSED caps, single-sourced here and GENERATED into the Rust codec by build.rs (generate_store_net_contract) so the guest and host cannot drift; a conformance test locks them, exactly as op-batch/canvas caps are locked. 'Fail-closed' means: on ANY breach the codec aborts the WHOLE frame and lets nothing partial cross the seam — the encoder throws before/without emitting a truncated buffer; the decoder throws and discards the whole frame (with a typed reason) rather than reviving a partial value. Every u32 length on the wire (jsonLen, segCount, each segLen) MUST be validated against BOTH the remaining buffer AND its cap BEFORE it is used to index/allocate. These caps are enforced in BOTH directions (request encode/decode and return encode/decode).

maxSegments.reason: Bounds the segment table, and therefore BOTH the number of byte-stream fields in one call/return AND the number of chunks one multi-segment value may be split into. 16 keeps the segment-count check cheap; at maxSegmentBytes each it is far past the maxEnvelopeBytes aggregate, so the envelope cap binds first.
maxSegments.reject: segCount > this is fail-closed (reason 'too-many-segments'), checked BEFORE any segment is read. An encoder that would hoist a 17th segment throws and emits nothing.

maxSegmentBytes.reason: 1 MiB ceiling on ONE SEGMENT — i.e. on one decoder allocation, NOT on one stored value. A value larger than this is split across segments and carried by the array sentinel form (see sentinel.multiSegmentValues), so this cap bounds allocation granularity while maxEnvelopeBytes bounds the value itself.
maxSegmentBytes.reject: any segLen > this is fail-closed (reason 'segment-too-big'), checked BEFORE the segment bytes are read/allocated; the encoder throws before emitting an oversized segment.

maxEnvelopeBytes.reason: 4 MiB hard ceiling on the ENTIRE encoded frame (magic + jsonLen + json + segCount + every segLen + every segment). The outer bound on total decoder allocation; deliberately >= maxJsonBytes + maxSegments*maxSegmentBytes is NOT required — this is a tighter aggregate cap than the sum of the per-part caps, so a frame that respects every per-part cap can still be rejected for exceeding the aggregate.
maxEnvelopeBytes.reject: a frame whose total byte length exceeds this is fail-closed (reason 'envelope-too-big'), checked on the whole buffer before decoding; the encoder throws if the growing output would exceed it and emits nothing.

maxJsonBytes.reason: 256 KiB cap on the JSON CONTROL PLANE alone (there is no such explicit cap on today's raw-JSON path; KBS1 adds one). Bounds the parse/allocation of the control plane independently of the binary data plane.
maxJsonBytes.reject: jsonLen > this is fail-closed (reason 'json-too-big'), checked BEFORE the JSON is read; the encoder throws before emitting an oversized control plane.

reasons.$comment: The fail-closed 'reason' vocabulary. On ANY violation the codec drops the WHOLE frame (never a partial value) and reports one of these stable string tokens. A host-side failure surfaces as an error result (ok=0 with the reason); a guest-side failure is a None/Err. Tokens are words (not numbers) so both codecs and any log agree on the same vocabulary.
reasons.bad-magic: the leading u32 != 0x3153424b ('KBS1') — wrong protocol, a cross-fed KEEL/KCNV buffer, or corrupt; check FIRST.
reasons.truncated: a declared length (jsonLen, segCount, or a segLen) overruns the remaining buffer, OR trailing bytes remain after exactly segCount segments (strict full consumption).
reasons.bad-json: the control-plane bytes are not well-formed JSON after length validation.
reasons.envelope-too-big: the whole frame's byte length > limits.maxEnvelopeBytes.
reasons.bad-segment-ref: a {"$b":N} sentinel references N outside [0, segCount), or a non-integer/negative N.
reasons.bad-sentinel: an object uses the reserved key '$b' with a malformed shape (e.g. extra keys alongside '$b', or a non-integer value) inside a KBS1 frame.

golden.$comment: store-net-bytes.golden.json (a later phase) will hold byte-exact vectors, each pairing a source (control-plane value + its byte-stream fields) with its exact on-the-wire KBS1 encoding as a lowercase hex string, mirroring op-batch-wire.golden.json / canvas-wire.golden.json. Planned vectors: an empty-segment BACK-COMPAT case (a segment-free call MUST NOT be a KBS1 frame — asserted as raw JSON, NOT hex here), an empty-value segment (segLen 0), a value containing 0x00 and 0xFF, an at-maxSegmentBytes value, a multi-segment frame, and an at-maxSegments frame. The Rust encoder is the oracle; a decoder reconstructs the source value structure-exact from the hex. The conformance chain and run instructions live in store-net-bytes.CONFORMANCE.md. NOTE: no runtime codec exists yet — phase 0 locks THIS schema + the generated constants only.
